subject: Climate & Environment
title: Tornado Alley
description: A micro-lesson that makes Tornado Alley usable.

hook.text: A strip of the central United States gets more tornadoes than anywhere else on the planet.

buildup.text: Tornado Alley stretches from Texas to South Dakota where hot Gulf air meets cold Canadian air.

discovery.text: The flat terrain and converging air masses create perfect conditions for supercell storms.

twist.text: Tornado Alley is shifting eastward — into more densely populated areas — as the climate warms.

climax.text: The Southeast now sees more tornado fatalities than the traditional Alley.

punchline.text: The danger zone is moving. The people in its new path aren't ready.

quiz.question: Why does Tornado Alley produce so many tornadoes?
options: Hot Gulf air meets cold Canadian air over flat terrain

details.summary: Tornado Alley is a broad region of the US Great Plains from Texas to the Dakotas where geographic and atmospheric conditions create the world's highest concentration of tornadoes. Recent research shows this zone is shifting eastward into the more populated Southeast.
details.whyItMatters: The eastward shift of tornado activity increases risk for communities with denser populations, more nighttime tornadoes, and fewer storm cellars than the traditional Alley.
takeaways: The Great Plains average over 1,000 tornadoes per year
Tornado activity is shifting eastward toward the Mississippi Valley
Southeastern tornadoes are more dangerous due to population, terrain, and timing

faq.question: Why is Tornado Alley located where it is?
faq.answer: Warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico collides with cool, dry air from the Rockies and Canada over the flat Great Plains. The Rocky Mountains channel upper-level winds to create strong shear, making this region uniquely tornado-prone.

faq.question: Why is the Southeast becoming more tornado-prone?
faq.answer: Warming Gulf waters increase moisture supply, shifting severe storm energy eastward. Southeastern tornadoes are more likely to occur at night, in hilly terrain that limits visibility, and in areas with mobile homes and no storm cellars.
